draft.title: The factor theorem
card: If \(P(a) = 0\), then \((x - a)\) is a factor of \(P(x)\). The reverse is also true: if \((x - a)\) is a factor, then \(P(a) = 0\).
To test a factor, substitute. For \(P(x) = x^{3} - 2x^{2} - 5x + 6\), we get \(P(1) = 1 - 2 - 5 + 6 = 0\). So \((x - 1)\) is a factor.
To factorise a cubic, try small whole numbers such as \(\pm 1\), \(\pm 2\) and \(\pm 3\) until one gives zero. Good numbers to try divide the constant term.
Care with signs: if \(P(-2) = 0\), the factor is \((x + 2)\), because \(x - (-2) = x + 2\).
draft.remember: If substituting \(a\) gives zero, then \((x - a)\) is a factor.

a.q: For \(P(x) = x^{3} + 2x^{2} - 5x - 6\), \(P(2) = 0\). What does this tell us?
opts: The remainder on dividing by \((x - 2)\) is 2
a.why: Because \(P(2) = 0\), the factor theorem says \((x - 2)\) is a factor. The factor \((x + 2)\) is the tempting wrong choice: it would need \(P(-2) = 0\), not \(P(2) = 0\).
a.clue: The factor has the opposite sign to the number that gives zero.

b.q: Mia tests \(P(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 4x + 12\). Which factor can she be sure of?
b.why: \(P(-2) = -8 - 12 + 8 + 12 = 0\), so \((x + 2)\) is a factor. The second option has the right value but the wrong sign in the factor. \(P(1) = 1 - 3 - 4 + 12 = 6\) and \(P(3) = 27 - 27 - 12 + 12 = 0\), so the last two options give wrong values.
b.clue: Check which number gives zero, then flip its sign for the factor.

problems.detail: P(x) = x³ − 3x² − 4x + 12 = (x − 3)(x − 2)(x + 2), so (x − 2) and (x − 3) are also factors. The question asks which factor Mia can be sure of, so a student who factorises fully could defend those options. The option '(x − 3), because P(3) = 12' gives a false value: P(3) = 0. Use a cubic where the distractor factors are genuinely not factors.

The why says (x − 2) has 'the right value but the wrong sign in the factor' and that P(3) = 0 makes the last option wrong. In fact (x − 2) is a factor (P(2) = 0), and P(3) = 0 shows (x − 3) is a factor too. The why contradicts the factor theorem the card teaches.
The why refers to options by position ('the second option', 'the last two options'), but the options are shown in random order. As listed, the second option is (x + 1), not the one the why means.

check.summary: Question b is flawed: the cubic factorises as (x − 3)(x − 2)(x + 2), so the distractors (x − 2) and (x − 3) are real factors, and the why wrongly dismisses them. The why also refers to options by position. Card and question a are fine.
